utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. If I could remind you once more of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence, which still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, good afternoon to you, sir. I am Mr. Momcilo Bulatovic, attorney-at-law, counsel for Mr. Sljivancanin. I will be asking you questions on behalf of the Defence team of Mr. Sljivancanin. I will try not to repeat any of the questions already asked by my colleagues. If you have any explanations to offer, please do so by all means. But one thing I do need to ask you is please make a pause between my question and your answer. Let's try not to overlap for the benefit of the interpretation unit and everyone else. I hope you understand that, sir. Mr. Covic, do you remember how many statements you gave in relation to the events in Vukovar in 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the number of statements, I don't really know. However, all I ever said were things that I personally experienced and saw. I told the truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, I did not ask you about the substance of your statements. I asked you about their number. Can you please remember who you gave these statements to, statements in relation to your experience in Vukovar back in 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically I gave statements to a gentleman from this Tribunal's Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: How many, please, if you can tell me?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a two-day session, two-day interview session. And after that we met yet another time, we went through my previous statement in order to enter some corrections. There were errors in typing, that sort of thing. So it was these gentlemen from the OTP who took care of that and I fully agree with their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me exactly when it was that you gave your statement, the two-day session, and when was it that you entered the corrections and amendments just to check whether everything was recorded faithfully and accurately?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really give you the exact dates, but this might have been about a month or a month and a half ago that we entered those corrections.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I told you that you gave your original statement in 2003?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's what the statement says, then it must be the case. The 5th of October, 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: November, you mean?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, October.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, do you remember giving a statement on the 14th of March, 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I gave no statements on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you not give any statement whatsoever in relation to human rights violations, civilian suffering, all the victims, and everything that you suffered in Vukovar back in 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what your question is based on or in relation to. It may be one of the statements that I gave to our various associations and institutions in Zagreb. After the camp, my experience at the camp, there were a number of people who requested statements from me; of course, I provided those. I shared my story with them. I told them the long and the short of it. I told them about the aggression against Vukovar and about the numbers of dead and injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Does the name Kezele Mara ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. First I hear of it. I don't know that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the usher to please show Mr. Covic a statement to look at. Just to check whether he's familiar with this statement. The statement contains a number of corrections, and I would just like to see whether he produced any of these corrections himself. This is dated March 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: It's in English?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's in English. But let me just look at the date. No, I don't think so. Possibly one of our institutes and associations that we provided statements to, I don't know. I spoke for Radio Zagreb twice, so this may be one of the reports or some such that they put together at the time. I know nothing about this transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can the witness now please be given the same statement in B/C/S, just to see if there is any information there that you may or may not have provided to the person taking this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, these are statements that were served on us by the OTP as statements given by today's witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will stick to my previous answer. This record, this lady Marija Kezele, she might have pieced this together by compiling the various things that I said for Radio Zagreb and the statements provided to those associations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, am I take that to mean that you never actually spoke to a person named Mara Kezele?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say. The simple answer is I don't know. Where we stayed as refugees there was a lady who came twice and talked to me. So this may have been Mara Kezele. Perhaps you should know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Where did she talk to you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my days as a refugee staying at the military academy in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, in addition to this statement that I've shown you, both in English and in B/C/S, there is a list there, please try to find it.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have it now. The list is right here, but one thing I can tell you for sure is that I was not the one who produced this list. If we follow the same logic, I can perhaps assume that this same lady, having talked to a number of us victims, put this list together.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, if you have the Serbian version or, rather, the Croatian version of this list in front of you, is it the Croatian version you're looking at?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The Croatian version, please. Could you go to page 8? I think he's looking at the English, isn't he? Could you please look at this paragraph down there, the names have been underlined. Can you please read that out?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The names of the local Chetniks have been underlined. The witness saw them commit crimes against Croatian prisoners. As for the others, he heard about them from neighbours, other residents and acquaintances, but he did not personally see them commit any crimes".

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This is a list that was I attached to your statement which leads me to conclude that you provided information on people whose names can be found on this list. People who committed crimes. Some of this information was based on hearsay; you heard from other people that some of these people committed crimes. Therefore, the names underlined on this list are the names of people who you personally saw committing crimes. Could you please look at all the names that are underlined and tell me if you know any of these people or should I ask you the questions?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the names underlined on this list, the first person I recognise is Capalo, Mirko Vojnovic. I saw him personally on his way into --

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You have explained that earlier on.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, I have. There is another person, Jezdimir Stankovic. I know this person. His nickname was Kesega. They called him Kesega around Vukovar. When we were standing in Velepromet outside those hangars he personally walked up to me, he knew me by sight. He is the son of the former manager of Vukovar radio and Vukovar's newspapers before the war. He had me lined up against the hangar wall, he picked up my wallet, or, rather, the money from my wallet. He threw my personal documents away, discarded them. I turned my head around and asked him to give me back my documents at least and asked him why he had thrown them away. He kicked me with his boot in the back. And said, "There you go. There, you have your documents." So that's what happened, and then he left. He was a TO member, but he was not wearing any sort of uniform. He was just wearing plain clothes, normal clothes. I can perhaps go through the list again. There are no other names that I recognise of people that I saw there. Probably there will be other witnesses who will be better able to do this for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, please look at the name under number 5.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Peko Pavlica. There is another man I know. His name is Pero Pavlica. This man was at the hospital entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You explained that already. So you don't know this man?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know a man named Pero.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So this might be an error or a typo?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, the statement in Croatian that you have in front of you that I have shown you, have you ever seen this statement before?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've never seen it before. This is the very first time I'm looking at it, and I must say I'm even quite surprised that such a statement exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This statement says that you actually signed it. Do you remember that, that's what the statement reflects?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. It was only when I talked to those ladies who came to see us. I can't remember. They were taking notes. I'm not sure if I signed anything or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, I thank you for this answer, but I would now like to move on to something else. What about number 30? The name is Boro Bogunovic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of this person?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I haven't. I don't know. I can't say anything, really. I don't wish to make a statement, if I simply don't know. The only intention I have is to tell the truth, so if I don't know this person, there is nothing I can say. No idea where this person was or what he did. I don't know. I'm sure I don't know this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, let's move on to some of the things that happened in Vukovar that are of relevance to me and to Mr. Sljivancanin's defence. You testified in chief that the so-called Croatian army at the beginning had some hunting weapons and a number of artillery pieces. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What sort of artillery pieces? Specifically, what kind and what calibre?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only heard about the artillery pieces from some acquaintances during my time as a refugee and in the camp. They told me that there had been a gun of some kind positioned at the Trpinja road. I wasn't told this explicitly, but my assumption that those had been anti-aircraft guns. Later on two tanks were captured, two JNA tanks. They had not sustained any substantial damage, so our defenders used those tanks for the town's defence. And that's about all I know about any heavy weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that the Vukovar's defenders had been receiving artillery support from Vinkovci. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, whenever this was possible, needless to say. But after we had been encircled for three months it was becoming increasingly difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, if you know, of course, how did this artillery come to be deployed around Vinkovci? What do you know about the origin of all this artillery?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I'm sure there will be other witnesses who will be able to help you with this. I think if you go and ask Mile Dedakovic you'd probably be better off because he was in command of those pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about the Varasdin barracks and what happened there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that. I heard that Croatia's defence greatly benefited from this because they managed to seize a lot of heavy weapons there which they used for the defence. I'm not sure about any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear these weapons were taken to Vinkovci and used to support Vukovar's defence?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody ever told me explicitly, but I imagine that this might have been the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday in answer to a question by Mr. Borovic you say said something about some logistical work that you did as part of Vukovar's defence. I think my colleague asked you a question about that, but I don't think your answer was complete about your support, logistical support you provided for the artillery there. I want to know a bit more about your role there, if you could please provide a more detailed explanation. What sort of logistical work did you do to support Vukovar's artillery?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer was not about artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking about artillery.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area where I was staying with our boys, the defenders, there was no artillery. All they had were hand-grenades which they used against tanks to defend from tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Covic. When you talk about what sort of weapons Vukovar's defenders had, you mentioned hand-grenades. Did they have any mines and, if so, what kind?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did have mines, and they laid these mines in order to prevent the attackers from getting through, thus aiding the town's defence to a great extent and making it possible for us to hold out for three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me where was it exactly that Vukovar's defenders laid these minefields, the locations that you're familiar with?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They lay these minefields in areas that -- where attacks were expected. Our lads did a pretty good job. It was a great help to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Were those personnel mines, anti-personnel mines, anti-tank mines or what kind of mines?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly anti-tank mines.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Was it laid down in accordance with a certain system, by people trained for that type of combat or was it dispersed throughout without any plan?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said -- you put that well. It was done without a plan. The minefields were dispersed around in those areas where tanks could have come across and where an attack could be expected. These young fellows thought this through and placed it appropriately.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, do you know that the defenders of Vukovar laid a road through a cornfield that was a secret type of road. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. A road ran through a cornfield. Mostly by night; that's when people travelled on that road. However, it wasn't possible to send weapons down that road, it was mostly medicine and equipment needed for the hospital that was sent down that road. People who stayed alive owing to that medication and equipment that came down that road ought to be very grateful for the fact that this road existed. I know this for a fact, because I spoke to a man who travelled that road bringing medical supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, in your statement given to the OTP as well as in this other statement which you say you had never given, although they are quite similar, you mention your activities supporting the defence of Vukovar, saying that you also transported the wounded. I would like to know how you transported them, in what type of vehicles?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we transported the wounded very rarely. If there was a lull in the bombing or shelling, then we would go and find a car or some other kind of vehicle, place a wounded person inside, and then rush to the hospital; however, those were rare occasions. Most often it was done by us carrying the people on our backs, in a very simple way. I personally saved the lives of two young men in this way. This is how we transported them most often. Very seldom we had a vehicle at our disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did ambulances arrive from the hospital to transport the wounded?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because they couldn't move around, they couldn't reach us. We had no way of communicating with the hospital to inform them about the fact that we had casualties. No, we had to transport these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. And since you were a person providing logistical support and advice to the defenders of Vukovar, you communicated with them, you talked to them and they informed you about what was going on. Do you know then how the defenders of Vukovar established communication with the others from those defence lines that you drew yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean defence lines?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The ones that you drew yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The defence lines were there. However, those of us who were in the rear, we had no communication with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, how did you, people who were in the rear, know about what the people at the defence lines needed?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, people would stay at the lines in shifts, you know. One set of people would be there and the others would come back and it was then that I was able to advise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, you told us that you provided logistical support telling them to dig deeper trenches?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The lines that you drew to us yesterday on the map of Vukovar, the one shown to you by my learned friend, Mr. Borovic, were there trenches drawn along that entire line?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were very few trenches dug out there because that area consists of urban settlement. There were streets and houses there, so there were very few trenches for that reason. However, towards the end of Bogdanovci, towards the hunting lodge, that's the area from which the tanks threatened intensely, and I was there with the defenders when that part of the town was shelled very intensely. This is why I asked them to dig out trenches as deep as possible along that line, which was about 500 metres long, in order to save lines. People keep thanking me to this day for giving them this advice. It was because of that that they survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you go to see how they dug out trenches? Did you go to give them any suggestions there on the ground?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I went there to see what they had done. I told them to dig deeper and also to dig wider, so that when there was a rain of shells they could hide themselves. I also told them that in areas where there were trees they should dig in a certain way to ensure better protection. This is how I helped them and advised them. The defenders were a bit angry at me for pushing them to do that. However, today they're grateful to me for this, because they believe that this is the reason why more of them survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you give them any advice concerning how to lay down anti-tank mines?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they knew about that. There was no need for me to give them any advice. They knew how to lay the anti-tank mines, and I told them if this is the way to do it, that's fine. If not, then you can change it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This last thing that you just said, you said if this is the way to do it, that's fine, if not, then you can change it. What were they supposed to change?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The location of an anti-tank mine, that's what they were supposed to change. This is an elevated area, and there are parts which are not accessible to tanks, because they are too elevated. This is why it was important for them to lay down mines in the areas that were lying a bit lower, thus accessible to the tanks. It was just a simple piece of advice.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that you went to the main defence staff of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you went there in order to draw for Borkovic, the commander, also known as Mladi Jastreb, certain things on maps. Would you please explain for us how come you were invited to do that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He invited me to come because once he took over the position from Mile Dedakovic, he realised that as he was not from Vukovar -- you know, he was from a place from a village near Zagreb, so he was not familiar with Vukovar. In this building where he was, he learned that before the war I was a member of the TO staff, and thus he believed that I was well acquainted with all of those issues, and since he did not know the town well, he asked me to explain to him where our defenders were, and from which locations the main assaults on Vukovar were launched. I explained that to him, I drew it on the map for him, and thus provided him assistance of which I am proud to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, do you know that somebody else from Vukovar, a national of Croatia, also had a rank of a reserve officer?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such people, but I wouldn't be able to give you any names because it's been 15 years now. But I know that there were such people. I know that there were a couple of people who were reserve officers and who assisted in other defence areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. These other people whom you know, did they also participate in the defence of Vukovar, just like you did?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that these people who I know, in view of their age, were able to provide advice. They were people of advanced age, thus they were not able to bear arms actively. However, they were able to provide other types of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: As a reserve officer of the Yugoslav People's Army, did you have a wartime assignment?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not have a wartime assignment. I had it back in 1968, and that has nothing to do with the issues we're discussing here. That was back during the period of time when an attack was expected on Yugoslavia as a result of problems in Czechoslovakia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you received notices to attend various types of manoeuvres and exercises. Do you remember when was the last time you were asked to come along?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in 1986 when I was called the last time. However, I had -- I developed pneumonia and because of that I requested to withdraw from the TO staff. That was the end of my involvement with the TO staff back then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us conclude. So in 1986 you ceased being a member of the TO staff. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke to us about the assistance that the defenders of Vukovar received and there was some misunderstanding there. Varasdin was mentioned and then Zadar, so let us clarify that. Let us not mention any cities but rather have you tell us from which towns the assistance arrived to the city of Vukovar, what were the numbers of people who arrived and what type of assistance?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zadar was mentioned here probably by mistake. Probably somebody misheard it. It was impossible for anybody to arrive from Zadar. You know where Zadar is, it's on the coast, and it was impossible for somebody to come there to assist people in Vukovar. It was mostly people from Varasdin who came to assist in Vukovar, mostly policemen from Varasdin and then also some people came from Nasice, from Nustar and so on. Some people came from Vinkovci, Zupanja, and those locations that were closer to Vukovar and fortunately were not occupied at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, can you tell us about the numbers of people who arrived. When you put all of these locations together, how many people arrived to assist in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on my assessment, I'm not sure, but I think between one-third and one-half. I don't know the exact number. All I know is that people arrived from Zadar -- no, I'm sorry, not from Zadar; I made a mistake. People arrived from Varasdin. There were 150 of them. These are the people who went to Stajicevo with me and were then exchanged from there, from the camp in Stajicevo, and it was then that I learned the exact number of them who had come to defend Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And what is the exact number, the one that you just gave us?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were 150 of them in the camp with us. I learned about the number accidentally. On one day eight persons from Varasdin were killed. They slept in a basement. And I don't know who killed them. Was it locals, members of the TO, or perhaps some of the Seselj's men. But anyway, somebody approached them, threw a bomb into the basement and killed all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, I didn't quite get an answer that I was looking for from you.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I am asking you to give us the total number of people who came to help you, including the 150 from Varasdin, Nustar, Nasice, Vinkovci and so on. What is the exact figure?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact figure. That's why I didn't give it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Covic, let me ask you this: Do you know whether there were any foreign nationals who assisted in the defence of Vukovar during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for foreigners, there were none, no. After the aggression on Vukovar -- or, rather, that was the first aggression carried out in Croatia. Therefore, there were no foreigners in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, I will now ask you about the names of some people to see whether you know them, whether you heard of them. And please tell me in relation to each name whether you know the person and whether you know something else about them. Franjo Kracak?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Martin Pliso?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Likewise, I know nothing. It could be perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, the name is not on that list. There is no use looking at that list. Stipe Pole?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Doesn't ring a bell. Doesn't mean anything to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Ivica Arbanas?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Ante Roso?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ante Roso, no. No, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Marijan Bodruzic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, no, nothing. I think that that last name indicates that it's not a family that comes from Vukovar. You know, I worked for the electric utility company. I knew a lot of family names living in Vukovar, and I don't remember hearing that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What about Ante Bodruzic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing. No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Petar Juric?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Velimir Djerek?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Stjepan Sucic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stjepan Sucic is a person from Vukovar; I know him. I knew his parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What else do you know about him, if anything?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was also a defender, but unfortunately that street before the war, it was called Zelena Street. When that street fell, his parents were killed. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I just wish to object for one moment. What is the purpose of a rehearsal of a lot of names? There doesn't seem to be any relevance at that time in relation to what appears to be a memory test.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, could you indicate briefly the relevance?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. It is with pleasure that I can indicate this. All the names I have mentioned were people who were in charge of certain units of the so-called Croatian army, the National Guards Corps and the Vukovar defenders detachment at the period in time relevant to this indictment. This witness being heard here today was in involved in providing logistical support for Vukovar's defenders in the way described. I find it is impossible that he has never heard any of these names. All the more because some of these people held important and prominent positions within those institutions and units that were in existence at the time. By way of clarification, Ivica Arbanas was the commander of the National Guards Corps in Vukovar. So much for relevance. But I was about to move on to a different set of questions anyway. However, I did notice the witness looking at his watch at one point, and in view of his poor health, I believe he may feel a need to take a break at this point, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be allowed to say something. I was looking at my watch and wondering why so many names. I thank the President because that was precisely what I was thinking about, why so many names, why go on with so many names. Who on earth would remember after all this time, especially since most of these persons appear to be quite young. How would I know these people? And I must say, I also agree that a break would be desirable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is very early yet for the break. Are you really feeling the need for that? You are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I feel fine today and, if necessary, we can do as you see fit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. We will carry on. Mr. Bulatovic, the objection made, I think, has shown to be displaced by the justification you have given. Now Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course I understand the reply given now that I see the relevance, but it is the corollary to the relevance that I submit is the essential issue. If, as my learned friend now appears to be saying that these are important people, is he going to be saying to the witness that he is not a person who performed the task or was in Vukovar or was involved in any way that they have alleged? He is entitled to be able to know exactly what the purpose of the question is and a chance to answer that, I would submit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would have assumed Mr. Bulatovic is coming to that. He seems to have just about finished his list of names or sufficient of it. And we'll see where he moves to now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I'll dwell on this one name that you appear to be familiar with, Mr. Sucic. The reason I'm dwelling on this name is because, Mr. Covic, in your statement, you described who Mr. Sucic was. Are you familiar with this person's nickname?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The only thing I do know is that he was one of the defenders and he was one of my son's friends. That is actually the reason I know him. And when this happened during the first heavy attacks on Vukovar, when part of Zelena Street and Radnicka Street fell and his parents were killed, he came to stay with us. He told us the sad story of how his parents had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the usher's assistance, please? I would like to show Mr. Covic the statement he gave to the OTP. Unless he already has a copy in front of him, which is possible. Mr. Covic, could you please go to page 3? Paragraph 6. Have you found that? Could you please look at the sentence that begins "the Sajmiste commander." Have you found that? Could you please read it out?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Please read it for us.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The commander of Sajmiste was Sucic, also known as Crni, but this is the very first time I hear the nickname."

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Covic. Let me ask you this: This is a statement you gave to the OTP. Did you sign this statement at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This statement I don't know. I don't think I have ever seen this statement, but all I can say is about Mr. Sucic, if you ask me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, allow me to remind you that this is the statement you gave to the OTP back in 2003. I am now about to show you the original statement, the English version, if the usher could please help me with this, just to see whether this is your signature, the signature being shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature. I confirm that. It's mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can we therefore conclude that you did state what you have just read out to us, this allegation that's part of your statement. It's not something that was made up by someone, is it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that my son told me about what Sucic was doing at the time, but that's about all I knew about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Covic, let's move on, please. When did your son join the break-through attempt?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but I believe this occurred on the 3rd of November. At this time our neighbourhood had already fallen, the 6th Proletarian Division neighbourhood. When the lads withdrew, they showed me the weapons. They all had a hand-grenade left, one each to kill themselves should they be captured and a handful of bullets, and my son was among the first to join the break-through attempt.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You talked about these people who kept an hand-grenade just in case. Was that all they carried on their way to the break-through or were these people who stayed behind in Vukovar carrying a single hand-grenade? I'm a little bit unclear about this. Can you please explain?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know why you are so unclear about this. It's very simple, really. These young people were anticipating that if they were to be captured they would be killed. They reasoned that they would never surrender. In case they were caught or captured, they would use the hand-grenade to kill themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to the hospital, Mr. Covic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic, before you do, you put this list of names to the witness. You, in explanation to the Chamber, have suggested the relevance of it. You haven't put that relevance to the witness to get his comment or observation on it. And it's that relevance which is the critical part of your defence case on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you are entirely right. My understanding, however, was that the witness knows nothing about this, that he's never heard of these people. I have already shown him these names, for example, Ivica Arbanas, who was the commander of the National Guards Corps, asking the witness whether he knew anything about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Your point, as I understood it, was, it would first be does he know or does he accept that they are names of defenders; and secondly, if they are, how is it that he doesn't know those names, if he was there involved in some way in supporting them with advice or providing food or the other things that he has mentioned. And I think those matters, if that is your position, ought to be put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, you said you're not familiar with Blago Zadro, or, rather, you are. He was the commander of Borovo Naselje?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you about Ivica Arbanas who was the commander of the National Guards Corps. Have you ever heard that name?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regrettably I must say I am greatly surprised by your questions. My duty here before this Chamber is to testify about crimes that I witnessed. As for this defence strategy, I don't think it is best served by questions like these. Whether I've heard of these people, where they were, I must say I find your questions rather strange. I'm sorry, but I have to say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, do you remember the name Ivica Arbanas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't remember the name. These were people who were quite young at the time and I didn't know most of them. It was by pure chance that I knew Mr. Sucic. I see this nickname being used here, Crni. I don't think I've ever heard that before. So that would be my answer, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, have you ever heard of the Eltz palace, the palace of Count Eltz?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I've heard of it and I know where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any members of the National Guards Corps or any of Vukovar's defenders positioned there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More for the most part the people there were civilians, as I said yesterday in answer to one of the questions I was asked. There were those enormous cellars there, and I mean, go figure, a single bomb dropped by a plane killed 12 people. There were a handful of defenders there who stood by and watched all the firing coming from across the Danube, from an area known as Dunavac, all this shelling of Vukovar, and they were there to take care of people, to look after people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry for interrupting, but the issue is perfectly straightforward and my learned friend is doing a wonderful minuet around the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Don't worry, Mr. Moore, I'm still there. It hasn't gone away. Mr. Bulatovic is still pursuing his point, I'm not quite sure in which direction, but if he doesn't, I will have to take over and do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it appears there is a bit of confusion between myself and the witness. We'll try to do better than this. I'll try to change tact now, since Mr. Covic doesn't seem to like the nature of my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, you were quite often at the headquarters of the National Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not often. I stated very clearly that I was there once. I gave a statement. You should be better able to remember what I said there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You said you were there you helped them read some maps, that sort of thing, so what I want to know is: Do you know how many people in addition to Borkovic were there who were in command of the Croatian forces, the National Guards Corps and all the remaining units, those who were at the headquarters itself?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several of them, but I didn't know anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Were you ever in touch with any of the commanders except this one single time when you talked to Mr. Borkovic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was only when I was in touch with Mr. Borkovic and we only met once. As for the other people, I was not in touch with anyone else, and I did not talk to anyone else. I have idea who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What about your logistical activity? Did it not come down to the area in which your son happened to be, Sajmiste?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, my activity covered that area. It's a very sad truth it was only us, three parents of three defenders, were there to feed them, and you are perhaps able to imagine what this looked like. There was no water, there was hardly any food to be had. We gave them some vegetables, but there was precious little to be had to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever have a chance to communicate with Stjepan Sucic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was only once that I had a chance to talk to him. He came to see my son, and he told us that his parents had been killed. But that was the only time I met Mr. Sucic. Later on, after my return to Vukovar, I met him several times. And he gave me a detailed account of everything, but I don't think that's of any relevance here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think there is any further need to ask about these witnesses, Your Honours. It is quite clear that the witness stayed in very limited area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. The impression gained by the Chamber is that he knew only two or three of the names that you read to him, but at the time, it is his evidence, he had contact with only two of them and then each on one occasion and he didn't have dealings with any other commanders. And the people there were young people whom were not social acquaintances, not known to him. Now, that's where the position lies as far as can be seen at the moment. If you want to do more about it, you may; but otherwise move on, as you were proposing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, that's all right. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps just one more question, and then we can have break. Not because of me, but because of the witness, if you should need one. The witness told us that he went to visit the trenches, to check how they had been dug out and also to inquire about the minefields and so on. Did the witness go there on his own initiative or did somebody ask for his assistance and urge him to go there and inspect all these locations?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody told me to go there. It was my personal wish. I wanted to go there for the simple reason that I wanted to help those young defenders survive, to ensure that they survived in greater numbers. They didn't know how to protect themselves and that's why I advised them and I'm proud of having done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. We have concluded with that. Let us now turn to the hospital. Would you please tell me when you arrived at the hospital? What time was it exactly? We heard several things, so let us just clarify that. What date it was and what time of the day.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We came to the hospital on the 19th in the early morning hours. I don't think there is any need for me to repeat. I have already explained how we approached the hospital and how much time we spent there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, I'm just interested in the time-frame to make sure that there are no misunderstandings. On the 19th, when you left the hospital, what time it was?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the early part of the night. I'm not sure what time it was, this is just my estimate, and that's exactly what it is, an estimate. I'm not sure what time it was. I didn't have a watch on me. However, it was night-time when we were transferred to Vupik first and then Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in Vupik, do you remember what time it was then?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We arrived in Vupik sometime at around midnight, perhaps 10.00 p.m., 11.00 p.m., just before midnight, but I'm not sure about the exact timing. However, it was early that evening when we came to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You said yesterday that you stayed at Vupik for half an hour and then you went to Velepromet. Then that must have been after midnight?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, something like that. We didn't stay there long. 45 minutes or so. And then very soon thereafter they separated 50 of us and then they started ordering us to cross the street quicker.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean, Mr. Covic, that it was on the 20th when you arrived in Velepromet, after midnight?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible, but it's not very likely. I think that we came to Velepromet before midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you be more precise?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You said that on the 20th at about 5.00 in the morning you were put on buses and taken to Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It was still dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us now examine this. During that period of time while you stayed in Velepromet in a location that you described to us, except for the two officers that you have mentioned, two officers of the JNA, did you see any other JNA officers?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw an officer. I don't know which two you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'll remind you, just in order to avoid any misunderstanding. As you told us, one was involved in that -- in that occasion when there were two Chetniks, and then the other one came when you were on the buses. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you this: At that precise moment when we were ordered to go to the buses, the office, which was across from the hangar, a lieutenant came out of that office. A lot of people were taken to that office and mostly they went in pairs or in groups of three. They would be taken out of that office and taken behind the hangar and killed there. The only thing I remember is that that JNA officer was a lieutenant and he had two stars on his uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe that in a bit more detail?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was night-time. I don't remember any details. I just remember seeing, based on his uniform, that he was a JNA officer, and again based on the two stars on his shoulder epaulet, I concluded he was a lieutenant. He went in one direction and we went in the opposite one. We boarded the buses and then were driven to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how many buses there were?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were very many buses. I can't tell you how many exactly. Once we arrived in Mitrovica, we stayed there for an hour by the prison, by the camp there, and then we were taken to a field which was about 500 metres or one kilometre away. And there were very many buses there as well. Later on we learned that some of the buses took people to Begejci and some took to our place, to Stajicevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a person with the last name Fot during your testimony, Darko Fot?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he is my nephew -- no, I'm sorry, I made a mistake. Kopf, Ivica is my nephew, whereas Darko Fot and his parents were god-parents to my wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. You gave evidence saying that you saw Darko Fot in the evening. I don't remember exactly what time it was.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was when we were taken to Vupik. He was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: How long after you had arrived did you see him?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you, when we arrived in Velepromet we stayed there for not more than 30 minutes and probably much less. And during that period of time he acted as I have described to you here and as I stated in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. It was on the 19th, in the evening, in Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the night of the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, do you think, Mr. Bulatovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem, Your Honour. I think this is a good time. I don't have many more questions left, but we can take a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think the witness has had a fairly good [microphone not activated]. We will resume at five minutes to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Covic, let us now turn to another topic, since we have concluded with the previous one concerning Velepromet. You said that there were a lot of buses who took you away from Velepromet, but you don't know exactly how many buses. Would you please tell us, did these buses enter the compound of Velepromet, or did they park in the street?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some were in the Velepromet compound. However, I remember that one stood outside, outside the gate. There were a lot of buses, and it was difficult for them to all fit in, so there were at least two buses outside of the compound and perhaps even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. It was night-time, I assume that you stood in front of the hangar and that you were among the first ones to board the bus?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The administrative building of that company stands between hangar and another building, and in front of it was a large area, and this is where the buses were parked.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: How long did it take for you to board the buses?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't take long. Half an hour at the most. And then we headed onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you left the compound. I would like now to show the witness photograph number 04672115. This is a photograph which was shown yesterday to the witness. It depicts Velepromet. Do you see it, Mr. Covic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please take a pointer or a pen, perhaps the usher can help you. Would you please draw on this photograph the location where the buses were, the buses that you boarded?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have told you, the buses were on the opposite side. And this whole area, there is a road here --

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And in which direction the buses travelled?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the direction of Negoslavci. However, I can't show you that on this picture. The road is here and then we turned and started travelling towards Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Would you please put an arrow and a number one next to it and circle the number one.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Since I assume that there were a number of buses there, do you remember which bus you boarded?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I boarded the second or the third bus, counting only the ones which were in the compound, and then there were prisoners here too, and most likely I think that I stood approximately here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Why don't you put number 2 next to that circle?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: From the moment when you boarded the bus and until you left the compound, you said that that didn't take long. Do you remember how long?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have told you, half an hour at the most, perhaps 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This area that you mentioned, was it lighted?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no illumination, it was dark. The whole city was without electricity. Even though this was close to the barracks, but there was a power outage in the city of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. I think we just need to clarify one more thing. Where did you board the buses? Was it in front of the hangar, or in this location that you marked with number 2?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This location that I marked with number 2. This is where I boarded the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, I'm trying to create an image in my head based on this photograph and what you said yesterday. Can you tell us, from the place where you stood in front of the hangar to the place, to the spot where you boarded the bus, what's the distance between these two spots?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It takes five minutes to cover that distance, or less than five minutes. I've been referring only to the time it took for everybody to board buses, and this is what I said lasted about 20 minutes. That's how long it took for everybody to board buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I tender this photograph with all the markings put by the witness into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, this exhibit will receive the number 151.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, reluctantly I have to go back to the statements you gave to the Tribunal representatives back in 2003. You said at the beginning of the statement on page 1 or 2 that you gave the statement voluntarily and that you were going to describe everything you saw and experienced based on your best recollection. This statement that you gave to the OTP as well as the addendum, which you created here when you came to The Hague, and the statement that you gave to Mara Kezele, the one that you have said you've never seen, and we shall investigate this further later on. In none of these statements did you ever mention the existence of the third officer in addition to those two that I asked you about. Therefore, let me put this question to you. This officer whom you described as a lieutenant, it was dark -- it was dark. Could this have been a member of the Territorial Defence, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's possible. It's quite possible. You are Defence counsel, and you should know better whether this was a member of Territorial Defence or somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you think that it's possible. Let me ask you this,

utterances.speaker: MR. COVIC
utterances.text: I omitted to ask you this earlier, and please forgive me for going back to this issue. Do you know a street called Sremskih Odreda is located?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. It.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: It's in Vukovar, in the neighbourhood called Sajmiste?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that whole area towards Negoslavci was referred to as Sajmiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So you have never heard of this street, Sremskih Odreda Street?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that street.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear about a shelter in that street, Sremskih Odreda Street?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that. I don't remember the street. I don't remember the shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Just another question, Mr. Covic. Do you remember what you signed, which of the statements you gave to the OTP you signed, what was the language of that copy? Did you make a request to sign something, or did you just sign whatever document was put in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I signed the one that we discussed. And everything that I said, everything that I spoke about, and all of this is in relation to that, I feel the better about that, because all I told was the truth, and I was glad to sign the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: But I'm asking you about the language of the statement which you signed.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement was in our own language, Croatian. You have it right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So this is the one you signed?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see the signature there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's right there. This is the statement that I signed. It's in Croatian. The statement is written in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wish to avoid any misunderstanding about this line of questioning. What I'm after is this: This witness's statement in Croatian, page 13, specifically, says that the witness confirms its authenticity, but it also clearly states that only the B/C/S of the statement is signed. However, the B/C/S statement that we have was not signed, or at least we are not in the possession of a copy that was signed. We just want to make sure that this is no mistranslation or anything like that. If we look at the statement in English, you can also find the remark that only the B/C/S version is to be signed, as it reads. But we do not have a B/C/S statement of this witness that is signed. This is a matter which we shall try to clarify in cooperation with our learned friends from the OTP. Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness, and I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Bulatovic. Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm not sure if this is a good time but the Defence would wish to raise a matter or, rather, a request. It's something to do with my learned friends from the OTP and something to do with the statements of this witness that we have been provided the documents in relation to this witness, yet we have heard today that this witness did not provide these statements, nor were they shown to him during the proofing sessions. I am talking about the statements given to Mara Kezele. My learned colleague Bulatovic discussed these with the witness in the course of today's session. This may be a good time to raise these matters because my learned friend is about to start his redirect, and what the Defence wants to know is what the source is for these statements, where do these statements come from, who did the OTP obtain these statements from. It seems that the Defence has been led astray on this issue. We were given statements that were supposed to be this witness's statements and yet today we have learned that these statements were never shown to this witness, nor has the fact that he was indeed the person that provided these statements been confirmed. In order to judge the witness's credibility, I think it might be necessary for my learned friend to indicate the source for these documents to us so that we can verify whether the statements were indeed made by this witness or not. That's all I wish to say, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. You will recall that the witness was able to identify his signature on one of them, one version of them. Yes. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I just deal with the concern by -- of Mr. Vasic. I take it that Your Honour is stating that this signature of the statement relates to what I will call the OTP documentation, that is my understanding of the signature, though it is in Croatian as opposed to B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You realise the Chamber doesn't have any of these documents so that we are not sure, but he did recognise his signature. I understood it was on a B/C/S or Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, that is certainly my understanding, and I know my learned friends have got a copy of it and the signature is there. I don't think they're suggesting he didn't sign it, but perhaps if I can just clarify that. The point seems to be it was not signed in B/C/S, but clearly there is a document signed in Croatian. I think my learned friend accepts that. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm afraid my learned colleague has not understood my point. I am talking about the statement that was done in English, the statement given to the OTP. We have a signature there whereby the witness confirms that the statement has been read out to him in Croatian and represents an accurate reflection of his testimony. What I said a while ago, there is something called witness acknowledgement, and just above you can see that only the B/C/S version is to be signed, unlike the English version. And the English copy reflects the same thing. But we do not have a B/C/S statement that was signed as seems to be indicated here in this portion of the statement that relates to the witness's confirmation. Since I am the one raising this issue, I would like to add this: As for the statement provided by the witness to a person named Mara Kezele, there is no signature there, but if we go through the documents given to us, it is indicated that the statement was given in Zagreb on the 14th of March, 1995 and that the witness signed it. We don't have that, however. We have a draft of a translation of this document, whereas I clearly asked the witness today about this, and the witness said that he did not remember ever talking to a person named Mara Kezele. He knows nothing about the person, knows nothing about the statement, and knows nothing about the list which was based on his own account, at least based on what this person Mara Kezele tells us. We don't have a statement that was signed. And that was the statement that Mr. Vasic was talking about. Because this was the statement that was furnished to us by the OTP as the statement of the witness, and I believe that is the gist of all this misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Bulatovic. Mr. Moore, can I say is it preferable to re-examine before there's some attempt to resolve this, or do you want to resolve? I am in your hands there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The witness should be re-examined in relation to what I will call the witness acknowledgement in respect of the -- what I call the English 2003 statement, and that can be read out or put to the witness, whether he agrees it's his signature and the content of that. In relation to what I will call the 1995 document which was furnished to my learned friends, they have cross-examined that statement. I did not adduce it in evidence. They cross-examined on it. They have got the evidence in relation to it, this witness's evidence. And I'm not going to re-examine in relation to that. Because, quite simply, he gives no evidence in relation to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, would you be kind enough, please, to look at something that should be on your screen, page number is 03437611. I'd like you to look at the screen, if it's possible. Mr. Covic, just forget about the documents. Just close the documents for a moment. Thank you very much. Just look at the screen for a moment, will you? Thank you very much. Now, you should --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's a very blank affair, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We've got it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now you've got something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You've got the screen in front of you, Mr. Covic, and you've got a -- the last page of your statement. Do you see that? On the screen.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's in English, but I can see it all the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could Your Honour forgive me one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this the one we're talking about? Or the other one?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: There is nothing on either of his screens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yeah, I have it now. November 2003, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If we just look at this particular page, do you see a signature there that is your signature?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is my signature, and I put it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And we've got the date which is, I believe, the 5th of --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The 5th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The 5th of November, 2003. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Just below your signature, we have an English translation, and it reads as follows, I'll read it in English, and the interpreters hopefully will interpret it for you. "This statement has been read over to me in the Croatian language and is true to the best of my knowledge and recollection. I have given this statement voluntarily and am aware that it may be used in legal proceedings before the International Criminal Tribunal for the prosecution of persons responsible for serious violations of international law committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia since 1991 and I may be called to give evidence in public before the Tribunal." And there seems to be a signature below that again. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's my signature too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Is it right that this statement that you gave to the office of the Prosecution, or Prosecutor was, as it says, read over to you, that it was, to the best of your ability and your recollection, true?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've seen the record. I had seen the record, I then signed it, and this is an accurate reflection of what I spoke to those gentlemen about on the given date, the 5th of November, 2003, and I must say I'm quite happy with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I just want to show you one final document, which is our page 03437616. It has been shown to you by the Defence. To assist the registry, it is a handwritten list. Now, can that be brought onto the screen, please? Unfortunately it's a very poor copy, as far as I can see, but can you see it all right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you write that document?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said at the time that I didn't, because this is not my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed, Mr. Covic. I would like to move on to some other topics, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It would appear desirable that those two documents be marked for identification, Mr. Moore, so that the record will enable reference to what it is the witness has seen and is saying on the one hand is my signature, and on the other hand is not my handwriting, should that be relevant at some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I, for my part, wasn't going ask for them to be marked for identification. The witness has given his evidence. If the Court of its own motion wishes for it to be done, of course the Court can do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will each be marked for identification, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The first document will be received under reference number 152 marked for identification; while the second document, which is the handwritten note, will receive the number 153 marked for identification. I thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies for interrupting my learned friend during his redirect, but it is now that the Defence is utterly confused. Can we please have some clarification about this document 03437676 marked for identification as 153. When was this document provided? Because we have never seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Was it not cross-examined on, Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have never seen a list like this. It was never served on us. A handwritten list. What my colleague, Mr. Bulatovic, based his cross-examination on is a typewritten text and bears no resemblance at all to this copy. ERN for this document is 00367756 and 00367757. This is the list which is part of that document that the witness failed to recognise on cross-examination and bears no resemblance whatsoever to the document that we are looking at now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. I think what that demonstrates is that I should have been alert to have that marked for identification when it was being used so there would be no confusion as to which document. But we are clarifying the matter bit by bit. The last document which is marked for identification 153, Mr. Moore, seems to be a stranger and is not the document which was put to the witness, it would appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The handwritten document, if I may use that phrase, 7616, is in 65 ter exhibit list, at exhibit number 14. That's -- that's the record that I have. And I've checked with our case manager, and it was served. I'm equally rather surprised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Being served is one thing. The point is, it's not the document that the witness was dealing with. The witness was being cross-examined on a typed document, not on this handwritten one, or hand printed one, so that at the moment it's not a document that was properly put to the witness in re-examination - no fault of your own - nor is it a document that needed to be marked for identification. What you haven't dealt with is the typed list that Mr. Bulatovic was cross-examining on, if you wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But they are the same exhibit. My understanding is Exhibit 14 is -- or compiles a typed list and a handwritten list. It is one and the same exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you saying the names are the same?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: As far as I recollect, they are. But I need to just have that checked absolutely thoroughly. But as far as I am aware, they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And are you saying that they each were provided in the 65 ter list as part of the one document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: My understanding is that's correct. They are the same exhibit. One is in a typed form, and one is in the handwritten form. One -- one seems to be a typed version of the earlier, if it be earlier, handwritten version. The witness has said -- I've worked on the basis that the handwritten will be the earlier document and consequently I have asked the witness whether he has seen this document or whether it's his. He says it's not in his handwriting. So as a consequence, I did not deal with the typed version because it has no relevance if it does not flow from the handwritten. But my understanding, as I say, is it is one and the same document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And are these all Exhibit 14 in the 65 ter, or Exhibit 14 in this trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I just clarify?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, they are the same. But they have a different -- a different ERN number. But the typed -- the typed and the handwritten are the same exhibit, and served on the Defence. The document that the Defence referred to, I'm told, is the same typed list, but with a different ERN number.
