So it seems to be that the source is the handwritten, which this witness says is not his, and therefore the typed clearly does not follow. With regard to the ERNs, there are two ERN numbers, Exhibit 14, my learned friends have had, that is handwritten and typed, but they have cross-examined on the same list but with a different ERN number. That is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think the Chamber will receive both typewritten lists marked for identification and then we will have all three, and people may want to do something about that in the future. At least they will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, do we have two typed lists?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That is what seems to be the case. There is 65 ter Exhibit 14, which has got at page number 7616 a handwritten copy of a list and it just says "Velepromet" and then particularises various individuals. Attached to that is a typed list which says "Velepromet, list of criminals/evil-doers." That is the same exhibit, Exhibit 14, on the 65 ter list, which was served. My understanding is that what the Defence are cross-examining on is a typed list which I believe I cannot -- I have not checked exactly, deals with the same topic, the same names, but in a slightly different form with a different ERN number. But the source document is the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And that different ERN number is?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will just get that for you, if I may. Would Your Honour forgive me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The number that I have been given are 00367756 and 57.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, that is a list which is quite different from 03437616, the handprinted one. That list contains 32 numbered names and information such as captain of this and so on. The handprinted contains 27 numbered names. And there is some other information on the right-hand side which seems to be additional names. So there is much more on the handwritten document than on the typed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, the typed that I have, and I know my learned friends have, which are 756 and 757 have 51 -- 51 names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is page 757 a continuation of 756?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I am assuming it is. Because at the very bottom of 756 you come down 31, 32, and then you go over, and you go 33, 34. It also has got number 2 at the top. So 756 and 757 are consecutive numbers, I would submit clearly the list, and my understanding as I say, and I have not gone through in the minutia that I offered, but my understanding, one is the typed version of the other. I see someone nodding in agreement with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, I'm going to do something we don't normally do. Mr. Covic, you have on the screen in front of you a handprinted list of names. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a list that you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember the list at all. I am certain that I did not produce this list myself. Whoever did, the list still wasn't shown, not to me. I can go through the names, and my conclusion is I may know perhaps two or three persons from this list, but not more. That would be my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. If, now, we could receive marked for identification 0367756 and 7, the two typed pages referred to by Mr. Moore, received as one exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document will be marked for identification with number 154.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. And could I say that our quick examination indicates that those two pages together contains all the names that are on the handwritten --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As far as we can observe in a quick observation, the two typed pages contain in total the same names that are on the one handprinted page. But we've not had time and I propose to do a detailed comparison for ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in relation to that typed -- not typed copy, handwritten copy, I did ask the witness whether it was his handwriting and he said it was not his handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I am aware of that, and I've gone a little further, but the witness in effect says he knows nothing of it. Yes. Now, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for assisting us to clarify this. However, it seems to me that we should look at the matter from another angle. Namely, these two lists, based on what I was able to see, resemble each other. However, the names and the order of names is quite different. Some names are underlined in one text and not in the other, and at the end of the list there is a comment concerning the underlined names, the comment that is missing in the handwritten version. Moreover, it is true that my learned friend provided to the Defence under number 14 on the 65 ter list a handwritten text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, nowhere in the title of the document or in the document itself can we find anything which would allow us to link it to this witness, Mr. Covic. No, on the contrary, it is stated that this is a list provided by the former prisoners or inmates. Following that, when we received this typed up version shortly before Mr. Covic came to testify, we were told that this is a document accompanying the testimony of Mr. Covic. So there was no way the Defence could have linked the two documents, which, as I said, are not identical. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think everything you've said about the list is borne out by our quick observation, Mr. Vasic. We are in the position at moment where the witness has been examined on the names, and he indicated two or three names which he actually identified, or names with which he was familiar, and he indicated how he knew those names. He has confirmed that when looking at this handprinted list. He says he thinks he knows two or three names only on the list, otherwise he does not know the document or the names. So whatever you may have been told about the list, it is not the evidence of this witness that that is his list. We have no evidence -- these lists have only been marked for identification in case at some later time it becomes an issue. They are not evidence against your clients in the case at this stage, as you realise. Well, I think that's about as far as we can go with this list at the moment. I'll ask Mr. Moore if he has further re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, yesterday you were asked about various individuals and you said that you "saw the son of my wife's uncle, Stjepan Petrovic, and he ended up at Ovcara." Do you remember giving that evidence? And I'm reading from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately, I do remember, and frequently I go back in my mind to what I experienced. I found him in the hospital, in the hallway. I asked him to be with me, saying that we would help each other. However, he told me that he was coming with me down to the basement where the wounded persons were to thank the nurses for treating him. His parents had some health problems too. He said he would come back immediately. I begged him not to leave, to stay with me. Unfortunately, he left and never came back. He was killed at Ovcara. He was found among the corpses and he was buried individually. It is very difficult for me to remember that event. He was a very special man in Vukovar. He was a museum curator.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: After the hospital, you have said you saw him in the hospital when you were there, did you ever see him at any time after that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he went down there to thank the nurses, we remained there waiting for him to come back. We got on the last trucks and he wasn't there. Once I left the camp, after the hospital and everything else, I went to his parents and his brother, and I learned from them that he had been killed at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I want to deal, if I may, with another topic. To assist my learned friends, on the transcript it's page 3525. You have told us about the 50 men being isolated and then lined up in front of the hangar. Do you remember your evidence about that? Just yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you went on to tell the Court that of those men they were being taken away and you said you then heard shots, that they were killed; you assumed they were killed. Now of the 50 people who were there, you told us that you didn't know many of their names. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But I want to deal with their faces. Did you recognise any of their faces as people that you knew before that day?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew most of the people by sight. I knew names of only several persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a person next to me called Fager [phoen] whom I knew because he was my neighbour and so on. Since it was night-time, I could just conclude that I knew some faces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want you to listen, please, very carefully to the question. I've asked you if you knew the faces before that night, and you said you did. What I want to ask you is this: Did you see any of those faces after you came out of the hospital and went back to Vukovar? Do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Didn't see what?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see the people who were taken behind the hangar towards the brick factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 50, line 8, I believe that my learned friend made a mistake when he said hospital, because he spoke about people being grouped in groups of 50. And that must have been at Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: My learned friend is absolutely right. Of course it's the hangar. I'll ask the question again. There is not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Covic, you've told us about the 50 people in the line, you said that you recognised many of the people, their faces. You've told us that. Yes?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, objection. Defence objects because Mr. Covic yesterday didn't say that he recognised the faces. He said that he didn't recognise them, and this is now a leading question from my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The question of what the witness identified about these 50 men was clearly raised in cross-examination. Mr. Moore is now pursuing that issue in re-examination. I think he has quite properly asked whether he was -- the witness is able or was able to recognise any of the faces of the 50 men at the time. That's an attempt to get to some clarification as to what the witness did know about these 50 men. If you read the transcript of the cross-examination, it was left, as I recall it, in a somewhat unclear state. So, Mr. Vasic, I cannot uphold your objection on this point. Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: To assist my learned friend, it's page 3525, and it's lines 17 to 19. When my learned friend Mr. Vasic's colleagues asked: "You could identify those people? "No, I didn't say that, I don't know their names. I knew many of them by sight."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So I will ask the question again, Mr. Covic. You said that you knew many of these people in the line by sight. And then you've told that they were taken away and you believe killed. What I want to know is: Did you ever see any of those people again, the ones who had been taken away?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP COVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't see them, unfortunately. Not even later upon my return from the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have no additional re-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Moore. Mr. Covic, you will be pleased to know, I'm sure, that that is the end of your questioning. The Chamber would thank you for coming to The Hague and for the assistance that you have given us. You are now free to return to your home. This would appear to be a convenient time to take the next break. And I understand that the next witness is a protected witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. And Mr. Smith will be dealing with that witness. I am told it will take 15 minutes, so it is a good waste -- a good use of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. We will resume at 20 minutes past 5.00 with the protective measures in place. And we welcome Mr. Smith to this trial and to the bar table. Mr. Covic, I thank you once again, and when we rise you will be shown out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on that card?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly swear that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, please sit down. If you could keep rather forward, it's important that the microphone in front of you picks up what you say clearly. You will understand that what you say will not be heard in your own voice outside this courtroom, and that your own image, your own face will not appear outside the courtroom. People cannot see it anywhere else. Mr. Smith will have some questions for you. Yes, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I would just like to first thank you for the welcome to the courtroom. The familiar accents and the familiar faces on the Defence side certainly make the transition quite comfortable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, I will first show a piece of paper to you, and it will have your name, your date of birth and the place where you were born. And can you tell the Court whether in fact that's correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I apologise for interrupt the very beginning of the examination. Unfortunately in the transcript, page 52, line 25, there is something that shouldn't be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, we have spotted it. It will be redacted. Yes, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, do you see that piece of paper in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are those details correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: Yes. Completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I ask that that pseudonym sheet, Your Honours, be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, as soon as it's seen by counsel. Mr. Smith, because of the voice distortion system, it's necessary that your microphone be switched off as soon as you finish your question. If you could try and remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have been warned earlier, and that was my first glitch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sure it won't be your last.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the pseudonym sheet will be exhibit number 155 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, you have received protective measures in this case in relation to your name, your image and your voice, so you can speak quite freely. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: Yes, fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask that we now be in private session to elicit a few personal details from the witness so that we don't have to break in and out as his evidence transpires.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, in 1991 did you live in that neighbourhood you just mentioned for the whole period of time before you left Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: No. Up until mid-August, when the shelling and bombing of civilian facilities started, up until that time they attacked only public facilities, water-tower and some other public buildings where they believed the Croatian soldiers to be stationed but they spared civilian facilities. In mid-August, they started bombing our neighbourhood and our civilian facilities throughout Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said they were bombing your neighbourhood. Who is "they," and can you describe the damage, if any, in your neighbourhood as a result of the bombing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: The planes belonged to the Serbian army or, rather, to the Yugoslav People's Army. The damage was quite significant. The roof was destroyed on my building and also the neighbouring building. And then that neighbouring building was on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you describe your building? Was it a single house or was it an apartment block?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: It was a residential apartment building with four apartments. I lived on the ground floor. The building was built quite poorly. They used concrete blocks to construct the building, and it wasn't really constructed properly. It was -- it could not withstand bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And if I can remind I just not to use the names of the people that are living -- were living in that building, that apartment block. But in relation to the building nearby that you said that was bombed, can you describe that damage, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: The neighbouring building also lost its roof. That was the house next to our building, and the entire house was set on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Once your building was attacked, what did you decide to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: It was in the evening, quite late. Perhaps 10.00 p.m. when the bombing started. When the situation calmed down a bit, I called Vesna Bosonac, who was my director. Above me a lady paediatrician lived in the building, so both of us talked to Vesna Bosonac. She sent a hospital car to pick us up and to take us to the hospital. However, we refused her offer. We told her we would come on the following morning because we had to gather some personal belongings that we would need with us. Therefore, in the morning, before the bombing and shelling started, we went to the hospital on our own.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And why did you call her? Was it to leave your apartment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: We wanted to leave the apartment because we believed it was impossible to go from work to -- from home to work. All of us were employed, all of us had our work obligations, and since the bombing started it was impossible for us to go from home to work every day. In addition to that, we were also scared. We believed our building to be constructed quite poorly, and we were proven to be right later on because most of those buildings were completely destroyed during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was your building a military target of any -- of any sort? Were there weapons in your building? Were you or others that lived in that apartment block in any defence or military formation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: There was no weapons either in my building or anywhere else in the neighbourhood. There were no military facilities there either. There were just civilians who lived there. Most of them worked either in Vuteks or in the medical centre, Velepromet, and Gradjevinar company. Those were prominent companies before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did Dr. Bosanac allow you to stay at the hospital? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: Naturally she allowed us. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And perhaps if you can just describe to the Court whether the kitchen was in the main building of the hospital or some other smaller building.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: No. The kitchen was in the old hospital building. There were three wards there, neuropsychiatry, ophthalmology, ear, nose and throat, and there was the paediatric ward upstairs. The washing room was still being used, and the cellar, and there was another section which is specialist surgeries for eye operations and ear, nose and throat operations?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And about how far was this smaller building from the main hospital building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: The smaller building was about 50 metres away from the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were those two buildings connected, and if they were, can you explain how?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: Yes. There was an underground corridor connecting the two buildings. The new building and the old building. There were two other small rooms, rather small, in the corridor, and that was the nuclear shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And this underground corridor that connected both buildings, can you tell the Court the two openings of the corridors, where they opened out in the smaller building and in the larger building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: In the larger building that depends on where you're looking from. But the openings were at the ends of both buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in relation to the emergency entrance at the hospital, where was the opening in relation to that of the main building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: The opening of the emergency ward was opposite the main entrance. At the opposite end of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if you can -- if I can run through the different floors of the buildings, in the basement of the smaller building, what were the two areas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: The two areas inside the smaller building were actually -- there were actually three areas: Neuropsychiatry, the ground floor; the first floor, the eye specialist and the ear, nose and throat specialist; and on the third floor, there was the paediatric ward.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And the kitchen and the laundry, was that in the basement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: The kitchen and the laundry were in the basement. But the kitchen used to be in a different building, which was demolished by shelling as early as September. It was entirely demolished so we had to set up a makeshift kitchen in those rooms in the cellar and each of these was no more than 20 square metres large.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And other than the shelling of the kitchen, was there any other shelling or attack on the hospital during those months that you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: During those months, heavy shelling continued, terrible shelling. It would only stop at night or die down a little, perhaps. But during the day there would be a continuing artillery fire at the hospital. There were air strikes too, occasionally. Early in October, if memory serves me, two bombs landed on the hospital. Although there was a huge piece of canvas in the hospital's courtyard with a red cross on it to indicate it was a hospital. They didn't take that into account at all. One of the bombs landed on the new building piercing through five ceilings before finally landing in the basement in this corridor connecting the two buildings, the old and the new. It landed right between the legs of a patient there. The other bomb fell perhaps 10 metres, 10 to 15 metres from the main entrance. It created an enormous crater, smashing all the doors, door-frames and windows on all sides. The only windows that were not shattered were those on the opposite side of the building. Likewise, the old building was entirely demolished, the windows, the doors, the whole thing. These could no longer be used. You could no longer be there in general. Therefore, we all decided to go down to the cellar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned that from the time you were at the hospital, basically mid-August until the 20th November there was heavy shelling and continuing artillery fire. Can you explain to the Court how constant that was or whether in fact it was irregular. Was it a daily thing or was it on a weekly basis? Can you explain a bit further?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: The shelling was constant, day and night. At night it would be a bit weaker, the intensity would be lower, and the same applied to most mornings. I would go about my work at night or early in the morning when the shelling was less heavy. Although I did this, on two different occasions a shell landed right behind my back and on -- I was thrown by this explosion into the air and landed five metres further away each time. My hearing has been impaired since, because my right ear-drum isn't functioning properly on account of these explosions, as a result.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And during this period, during this three-month period, was the hospital functioning as a hospital, and if so, about how many patients were inside, if you are in a position to estimate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: I think the hospital continued to function throughout until the fall of Vukovar. There were about 700 patients and staff. Once the -- those seriously wounded had been treated and helped, they would be taken to the warehouse or the nuclear shelter at Borovo Komerc because they had received some medical assistance and their lives were no longer in danger. This was done in order to make room for new wounded because every day about 80 wounded would be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And was the hospital used for any other purpose apart from helping the sick?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: No. Not at all. No other purpose. It wasn't used for anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And are you aware, during that three-month period, there was some Croatian defence of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: No. There were no Croatian defenders at all. There were people from the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior, two officers guarding the hospital entrance. They were positioned -- two of them were positioned at the entrance to the emergency ward, guarding the entrance, and across the way there were two guarding the old building, the one I have mentioned. However, members of the National Guards Corps would come every now and then. There were about 10 of them who were there throughout, at the hospital I mean. They would rotate, they would bring in their -- some of their own who had been wounded or perhaps when they were resting they would come to the hospital to visit some of their wounded mates. They did go into the hospital compound, but they were not allowed to enter any of the wards armed because those six officers that I have mentioned, six MUP officers, disarmed them on their way in, and they were given back their weapons on the way out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And from working in and throughout the hospital, as you have described, over these three months, can you give the Court an estimation of the numbers of national Croatian guards that you mentioned that were visiting other patients at any one time? Can you give some sort of estimate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: Yes, I can. There were about a dozen at any given point in time. Some were bringing in wounded, some were there to visit some of the wounded. I don't think there were at any time more than 10 a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was the hospital ever used as a military facility to store weapons or as an attack staging-post or anything of that nature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: Certainly not. The hospital did what it was supposed to do and there was only medical work being performed there. That was all it was used for.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned that you left Vukovar on the 20th of November, 1991. I'd like to talk about the day before you left now. When we look at the 19th of November and you think back, can you tell the Court anything unusual that happened that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: The unusual thing that occurred was Vesna Bosonac came. She visited all the units in the early afternoon hours, all the work units, in order to inform us that Vukovar had fallen. Just after she had left, I can't say if it was an hour or two later, perhaps, the army came in as well as the paramilitaries, they entered the hospital. Vesna Bosonac, as she was doing the rounds of all the work units, clearly told us that Vukovar had fallen and that all would be allowed to go wherever they wanted to go. Those who wished to go to Serbia could go to Serbia, and those who wished to go to Croatia could go to Croatia. She said a list would be drawn up and that's what eventually happened. After Vesna had left, soldiers and the paramilitaries came in. I was also in charge of building a fire in the kitchen. You can imagine how unpleasant it was. I was building this fire, and there was a man standing right behind my back carrying a machine-gun. It was really a most unpleasant situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And just before we talk about this man in the kitchen, you said the army came in. Which army came into the hospital, and do you know the paramilitaries that came in, the name of the groups?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: For the most part most of the paramilitaries were local Serbs. They were not carrying -- they were not wearing the regular military outfits. Some of their clothes were perhaps part of a military uniform, the caps perhaps or so, but there were a number of real soldiers among them. Real soldiers could be distinguished from the rest by the fact that they wore olive olive-drab uniforms, the JNA uniforms. And they were a great deal more orderly than the paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can back to the man that had the machine-gun that was present as you were setting fire to the -- setting the fire in the kitchen, can you explain what happened there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: He didn't do anything. It was just a very unpleasant feeling because I had this machine-gun pointed at my back. This was a regular JNA soldier. He wore the standard-issue JNA military uniform and a helmet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you continue to set the fire? Did he stay for a long time, or did he leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: Yes, I did. He lingered, and he monitored my actions throughout, but he didn't do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: During that afternoon or evening, did you come into contact with any other JNA soldiers, and if you did, can you explain how that happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: Regrettably, there was a very unpleasant encounter. I was taking a break, it was between 3.00 and 4.00, there was still daylight. I left by the exit of the old building into the courtyard. I reckoned that Vukovar had fallen and the war was no longer on. I nearly started crying because I had just reached the conclusion that I would probably be compelled to leave my town, the town where I grew up and spent my best years. I was asking myself the question all the time: Who on earth has the right to drive me out of my town? Within the hospital compound there were Jovica Komadinic, a doctor, his wife Gordana. His wife was a Croat and he was a Serb. Dr. Sego was there too - her married name was Antic - with her husband. And hen later another lady doctor arrived. Njegic, the paediatrician. There was a soldier walking in my direction. He said his name was Captain Sasa. He was smiling. He was accompanied by two Chetniks with beards. They were led by Bogoljub Riznic. I was his boss. He was a truck driver at the hospital. Captain Sasa said that they were the liberators. My reaction was quite gruff. I wasn't just being brave, but I reckoned the war was over. There would be no killing and no torturing people, so I was quite open when I told him -- what I told him when I gave him a piece of my mind. What sort of liberators are you? What have you liberated us from? Are liberators supposed to be doing the sort of thing that you're doing, destroying the entire town? He just smiled at me and answered that it wasn't the JNA that did this, but the Chetniks, and he pointed out two of those to us, those men with beards, unshaven men with cockades. They just smiled. I showed my revolt by making a sign at them. And before that he said that unless the Croatian army surrender their weapons, they would proceed and go all the way to Zagreb. After that I sort of cocked a snook at them, at one of them, the man who had introduced himself as Captain Sasa. I told him that the Croatian army and Tudjman would never surrender their weapons to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And so how did that encounter end up? What did Captain Sasa or any of these other men do after you said that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: It was after I told him this that I realised that perhaps I shouldn't have. The Captain Sasa was taken aback. He was surprised at my courage, the courage I had to face him and tell him that. Probably he liked me, in a way, because I stood up to him. So he ordered that driver, whose boss I used to be, to give me a packet of cigarettes because I was a hard smoker at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And you referred to earlier a Mr. Riznic, I think it's Bozo Riznic. What was he doing there with Captain Sasa? Were you able to understand what his role was, and who he was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: Bozo Riznic was one of my underlings. He was a truck driver and I used to be his boss. When Captain Sasa arrived, when the army stormed in, Captain Sasa took him to all the work units, and when I was with him he took him to the laundry room to show him where the two MUP officers from the old building had hidden their weapons and the uniforms after they changed into civilian clothes, and he happened to know this because his wife had worked in the laundry room.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can we just talk about Captain Sasa for a moment? What military group was he from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: From the JNA. He introduced himself as Captain Sasa. He held the rank of captain. He was looking very neat, very orderly. He had a thin moustache, he was clean-shaven, and he generally looked quite well. A real soldier. He had the appearance of a proper soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the uniform he was wearing, was it a JNA uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: Yes. JNA uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, in relation to -- I think you mentioned two other Chetniks. Are you referring to them as paramilitaries or some other people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: The paramilitaries of course because they weren't wearing military uniforms, they were very disorderly, they had the remains of food in their beards, crumbs. They were extremely slovenly, sloppy. This was 15 years ago, so my memory is not as good as it was. Maybe they wore the military trousers, the uniform, and not the jacket. But they certainly weren't members of any regular military force.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Court the relationship between those two paramilitaries whom you referred to and Captain Sasa, whether there appeared to be a relationship, whether they appeared to be his boss or Captain Sasa appeared to be their boss? Can you give some understanding of how they're related.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: It is certain that Captain Sasa was their superior because they did whatever he told them to do. He told Riznic to give me a carton of cigarettes. And when he told me that it was the Chetniks who had demolished the city, he pointed at the two of them and he smiled, just like they did. They just stood there. They weren't doing much because all they were doing at the time was just having a good laugh at all the things that he was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And after that conversation occurred, did they subsequently find the weapons that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you see Captain Sasa again later that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: Yes. About three-quarters of an hour before the last encounter I came to the kitchen all agitated and depressed because of the things that Captain Sasa had told me, that they would go all the way to Zagreb unless the Croatian army surrendered their weapons. I was complaining about my foul mood and about my dissatisfaction to one of my colleagues there who was the boss of the kitchen section, the food section. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: (redacted) They started talking about politics, as it were. We were slightly gullible because we failed to understand what he was driving at with all these stories, so some people were a bit too relaxed, should I say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If I can just stop you there for one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think a nickname was mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There is a nickname mentioned and there is a description of his recording a song for Radio Vukovar, each of which I think should be redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That would be appreciated, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sir, do understand, we're just ensuring that anything that might identify you is removed from the written record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I got carried away for a moment there. I will try to give adequate answers from now on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The answers were quite adequate; it was just a slip of the tongue. Witness, you mentioned that Captain Sasa was with Nedeljko Vojnovic. Can you explain to the Court who Nedeljko Vojnovic was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: And you also referred to a Bogdan Kuzmic that was with Captain Sasa. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: Bogdan Kuzmic was a hospital employee; he was a janitor. He worked at reception. However, as early as June he left work and went to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was he wearing? What was Bogdan Kuzmic wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: Bogdan Kuzmic was wearing a military uniform. He wore a helmet and he had that military long coat. And I'm no longer sure. It's been 15 years since, but it looked very much like a military uniform, the full set.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned that Captain Sasa started to discuss politics. Can you briefly describe what happened and how it finished?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: He spoke against Tudjman, he said that they were the liberators and then we opposed that. We said that they were not the liberators; we didn't call them and come and liberate us. It was a spontaneous conversation about war. One of them, I don't know how he ended up in the kitchen, I guess because Vukovar had fallen, so he was in the kitchen. His name was Slobodan. He was a Serb, but he served in the Croatian army. He said while he was at the positions he was a bit tipsy. And he kept on talking and Captain Sasa listened to him, and 10 minutes after they left, people came to fetch him. They took him away and he never came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you say "people came to fetch him," are you able to say who those people were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: I think, I'm not sure, that it was Bogdan Kuzmic, I'm not sure. At any rate, a person came to fetch him. A person came, called out his name, he responded, left the room, and never came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And do you know Slobodan's surname?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: No, no. Because he came to the kitchen. We ourselves kept wondering who he was. He introduced himself as Slobodan, said that he was serving in the Croatian army at the front. He didn't say anything else. I don't know. Nobody knows how he ended up in the kitchen, but after Vukovar fell people kept streaming towards the hospital. They believed the hospital to be the safest place after the city had fallen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And since leaving Vukovar have you ever heard of Slobodan again as being alive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: No, no. Absolutely not. Whoever was taken away, and it wasn't just Slobodan who was, whoever was taken away while Captain Sasa was there that evening and Kuzmic, Slobodan, and there were 10 people in that category. I can give you their names, if the Chamber wishes me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Perhaps if we keep going through your testimony you will have an opportunity as the time arises.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that lists where drawn up in the hospital to see who wanted to go where, who wanted to go to Croatia, who wanted to go to Serbia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: Yes, correct. The head of the kitchen drew up a list of the kitchen staff and the head nurse did the same for various wards. The lists were given to nurse Biba, who was the head nurse at the hospital. Her full name was Benazija Kolesar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And was it your understanding that as a result of those lists you would be evacuated on the following day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: Yes. That was my understanding, that everybody could go wherever they wanted to. Vesna Bosonac said that evening that we could go where we wanted, whoever wanted to go to Serbia could go there, whoever wanted to go to Croatia could do the same, so I believed that to be a settled matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: After your conversations with Captain Sasa and others, did you finally get to sleep on the night of the 19th to the 20th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: No. Nobody did. Myself included. Everybody was really agitated, we had spent the previous three months in the hospital working a lot, 16 hours a day, with the shelling and bombing going on. During those three months, I even prayed to God for a shell to hit me and kill me immediately. Therefore, the people there were all agitated. They realised that there was no war any longer and that they could go back to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you get some sleep that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: A bit. But mostly I was awake.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In the morning on the 20th what was the first activity you were involved in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: In the morning at around 7.00 we distributed breakfast. After that we waited to be told what to do next. I think that at around 9.00 they came to us and told us to go to the main emergency entrance, which is what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who was "they"? Who told you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: Some of us. It's been 15 years, I don't remember any longer. But it was a member of medical staff who had come from the main building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how did you get from the smaller building where the kitchen was in the basement to the main building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: We took the underground corridor, passed through the laboratory, went into the hallway of the clinic, and reached the main surgery entrance. Prior to that we passed next to the Crisis Staff and the plaster room where Major Sljivancanin gave a speech to the medical staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In the underground corridor, was that empty or full? Can you describe the situation there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: The corridor was empty except for us who were streaming out. Those were mostly technical services. Kitchen, laundry room and so on. Auxiliary services. We passed through. We were not considered medical staff. I saw Mr. Sljivancanin at the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Was the underground corridor ever used for patients to stay because of overcrowding?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: It was used throughout the war. Even though it was not an atomic shelter, there were only two rooms that were considered atomic shelter. They were next to the corridor, whereas the corridor was just a regular type of a corridor where seriously wounded persons were. They had special beds there. As I was leaving and going through the corridor, I realised that there were almost no patients there left. Almost everybody had been taken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were those patients there the night before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And about how many patients were in that corridor, can you estimate, say, the night before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: In that corridor there were perhaps a hundred or so patients. People were not evacuated only from that corridor, but also from the corridor of the clinic and that of the internal diseases ward. All corridors had serious patients -- seriously wounded patients lying there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said at this time Major Sljivancanin was giving a talk to the medical staff. Did you see him or did you just go -- were you aware that that was the case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: I didn't know that. When we came to the main building, we had no idea what was going on there. They told us to go to the main entrance of the surgical ward or, rather, the emergency ward, and I saw Mr. Sljivancanin at the door of the plaster room. I saw many of my friends and colleagues who were medical staff there. I saw him giving a speech to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Had you ever met Major Sljivancanin before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how did you know it was him then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: I saw him during that day; I saw him another three or four times that day. Later on I saw him in our papers and I realised that that was Mr. Sljivancanin. In addition to that, he also introduced himself several times, saying that he was Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you got to the main building, you went through the corridor, passed the plaster room. Did you leave the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: I didn't. Or, rather, I did leave the hospital. However, I went through a gauntlet. I had to go through a gauntlet created by regular army soldiers who searched our personal belongings. Then they directed us towards the five buses, which stood in Gunduliceva Street. I believed that we were going to a place where they would examine us, or talk to us. I had no idea where they were taking us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And why did you believe that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And why did you believe that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: I don't know. They separated us aside, the men. I believed that they would be questioning us about weapons, whether we had any weapons and so on. That's what I expected. I didn't expect anything bad to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And which exit did you leave from the main building of the hospital before you went through this -- I think you say a gauntlet of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: I went out through the entrance of the emergency ward or surgical ward.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Is that the -- is that the location where the ambulances come into the hospital with emergency patients?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Trauma patients were brought there, people with fractured bones, people who were in car accidents, and so on. This was the entrance for people who were seriously wounded and trauma patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you talk about regular army soldiers, you mentioned earlier JNA soldiers, paramilitaries. Which group did these soldiers belong to, or any other group for that matter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: They were members of the regular army, the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned there were a number of soldiers there. Can you give an estimate of about how many soldiers were involved, JNA soldiers were involved in this searching process as you left towards the buses.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there were five on one side, and five on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So without going through the particular names of people that went on the bus with you, can you tell the Court what you believe the ethnicity of the people that went on to the buses with you was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: Almost all of them were of Croat ethnicity. Perhaps there were a few Ruthenians there, and Serbs. There were some there. However, the majority were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what types of groups were you aware of went on to these buses? You worked at the hospital. Were there other hospital workers going on the buses, and were there any other types of groups that were being put onto these buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: Four or five buses - I'm not sure exactly how many there were - were already full. As I have told you, we were among the last ones to be informed and among the last ones to go to the buses. Therefore, I didn't see what happened prior to that. I was among the last ones to board the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: On the bus were there any soldiers or guards, people keeping you on the bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: Just a driver of the bus. There was a soldier at the door guarding us. So there were two soldiers, but regular soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say "regular," are you referring to JNA soldiers again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: Naturally, the JNA soldiers. Because they were different from other people. They wore the olive-drab JNA uniform and they looked decent, they looked orderly, just like regular soldiers do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The driver on the bus, could you say whether he was a civilian person or a military person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: Military person.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And was he a paramilitary or was he a JNA soldier or what group did he come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: A JNA member.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned that the bus was guarded by a JNA soldier. Did he also travel on the bus when you left the Vukovar Hospital or did he stay at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't remember that. I went to the back because the bus was so full. Originally it was supposed to carry 50 people, and there were perhaps 70 to 80 of us on the bus. Therefore, I simply didn't look any longer whether he went with us to the final destination or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when the bus left, did you -- did it travel with the other buses or did you go by yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: All together, all five or six. I don't know whether there were five or six buses, but all of them left together.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And I think you said earlier you thought you were going for some sort of interrogation, is that correct, or interview?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's what I said and that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And whilst you were travelling on the bus, were you ever told where your final destination was going to be by say the bus driver?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: No, nobody said anything. We just kept looking at each other, wondering where they were taking us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you tell the court how you were -- what you were thinking and how you were feeling at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: Not yet. I still wasn't feeling any fear. I thought they were taking us somewhere for questioning. I didn't think anything bad would happen to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court where the bus finally ended up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: Finally that bus, along with all other buses, ended up in the Vukovar barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say the Vukovar barracks, which barracks are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: The JNA barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how did you know it was the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: How did I know? I grew up in that city. I knew every square inch of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you arrived at the barracks did the buses park outside or did they go inside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: The buses entered the compound and parked in a semicircle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And once they parked, can you explain to the Court what you saw inside the barracks, what you saw outside of the buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: Once the buses parked, the local Serbs started approaching the buses. I thought, well, thank God, some of them were my friends, and I thought that they had not taken part in these evil events. All of them, however, showed up at the barracks. In addition to them, there were some volunteers from Serbia, Arkan's men, and Seselj's men, but among them there were also some local Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: These local Serbs, were they armed or in any sort of uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: They were armed. They had knives that they threatened us with. They went from bus to bus threatening to slaughter us, kill us and so on. They were dressed in different clothes. Some had fur hats, some had beards, some had the top part of a uniform or the bottom part, not a full JNA uniform, but perhaps just a portion of it. Those were paramilitaries. Among them were some JNA soldiers too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you say Arkan's men were there and Seselj's men as well, were they armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what about the JNA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you tell us the number of these local Serbs and Arkan's men and Seselj's men, about what size that group was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-012
utterances.text: In my assessment, about a hundred or so of them. And they all gathered around the buses. Some were coming up, some were leaving. It was quite a large group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, I am trying to judge the time. We've had a disrupted time programme again today because of the earlier witness. And we've really just about run the time we can run now. If you could identify a convenient time to stop, it may be now, as I sense you're about to get into something more significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct. I think now is a good time. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. I think what we'll do then is adjourn for the evening. We will resume tomorrow at 2.15. If you understand that, sir. We're finishing for the day now and we'll continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I understood that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 3rd day of February, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
